title: Covering Cracks in Content Moderation: Delexicalized Distant Supervision for Illicit Drug Jargon Detection

problem.claim: Social media platforms need to moderate illicit drug content, but drug jargon makes this difficult.

gap.claim: Existing term-list approaches are vulnerable to word substitutions and cannot reliably distinguish drug-related euphemisms from benign uses, while manually annotated training data is expensive and can become obsolete.

contributions.claim: JEDIS detects illicit drug jargon by analyzing contextual information.
JEDIS combines distant supervision and delexicalization to train without human-labeled data and address new terms and euphemisms.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe the combination of distant supervision and delexicalization as a novel approach.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On two manually annotated datasets, JEDIS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art word-based baselines in F1-score and detection coverage.
Qualitative analysis indicates that JEDIS is robust against pitfalls faced by existing approaches.

narrative_sequence.summary: Drug sales and discussions have become commonplace online as drug-related concerns rise and social media expands.
Moderating drug content is difficult because of the large amount of jargon used in discussions.
Term-list approaches can be evaded, misinterpret euphemisms, and depend on costly, potentially outdated annotations.
The authors advocate contextual moderation and present JEDIS, which combines distant supervision with delexicalization.
Experiments and qualitative analysis are reported as showing improved performance and robustness.

source_observation.claim: The proposed framework uses context instead of relying on a banlist and combines distant supervision with delexicalization.

interpretation.claim: Contextual and delexicalized signals may reduce sensitivity to surface-form substitutions and ambiguous euphemisms.

application.claim: For moderation tasks involving evolving coded language, consider context-based detection with weak supervision and lexical abstraction.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether this approach generalizes beyond the reported drug-jargon setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, model architecture, training procedure, or evaluation protocol.
The abstract does not quantify the reported F1-score, detection-coverage improvements, or qualitative findings.
The abstract does not establish performance outside the two manually annotated datasets.
